title: Pancake Sorting
description: Sort an array using only prefix-reversal flips, with a selection-sort-style two-flip-per-round strategy.

blocks.text: Given an array of distinct integers arr, sort it using a series of pancake flips. One flip picks k (1 to arr.length) and reverses the prefix arr[0..k-1]. Return a sequence of k-values that sorts the array, using at most 10 * arr.length flips. This document uses one specific deterministic algorithm and shows its exact flip sequence and resulting output.

blocks.caption: Each round finds the largest unplaced element and flips it into position at the back of the unsorted region.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","arr[] (distinct integers)"],["Flip operation","Choose k, reverse arr[0..k-1]"],["Output","A sequence of k-values whose flips sort the array, within 10 * n flips"]]}

blocks.text: Only being able to reverse a PREFIX (not swap arbitrary elements) is the defining constraint. The classic technique, "pancake sort," mimics selection sort: repeatedly find the largest element in the still-unsorted region, then use exactly two prefix flips to move it into its final position at the end of that region.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Two flips bring any element to any prefix-boundary position: one flip brings it to the very front, and a second flip (of the whole unsorted region) sends it to the back of that region.

Picture a stack of pancakes of different sizes, all disordered. The only tool available is a spatula that can flip the top k pancakes over at once. To sort them (largest at the bottom), repeatedly find the biggest pancake not yet correctly placed, flip it to the top of the stack, then flip the whole unsorted portion to send it down to its correct position at the bottom of that portion.

blocks.caption: Two flips move the biggest unsorted pancake to the bottom of the unsorted region.

items: For each round, the "unsorted region" shrinks from the full array down to size 1.
Find the index of the largest value within the current unsorted region.
If it is not already at the front, flip it there first (one flip), then flip the entire unsorted region to send it to the very end of that region (a second flip).

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The complete flip sequence is [3, 4, 2, 3, 2], and applying it to [3,2,4,1] produces the fully sorted [1,2,3,4], well within the 10 * 4 = 40 flip limit.

The direct implementation always performs the full two-flip pattern (flip to front, then flip to back) for every round, even when the largest element happens to already be at the front of the unsorted region (in which case the first flip is redundant but harmless).

A small refinement skips the first flip entirely when the largest element is already at index 0, saving one flip per such round without changing correctness, since the element is already positioned to be sent to the back with just the second flip.
Always perform both flips (to front, then to back) every round, even when the largest element is already at the front.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","n rounds, each scanning up to n elements and performing an O(n) flip"],["Flips used","Up to 2n","Two flips per round in the worst case, always performed"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This is already within the allowed 10n flip budget; the optimization below is a minor practical refinement, not a different complexity class.

Skip the first flip (to bring the max to the front) whenever it is already there, saving one unnecessary flip per such round. The overall algorithm and complexity remain the same, but the flip sequence is slightly shorter.

items: For each round, find the largest element's index in the current unsorted region.
If it is already at the very end of the region, skip this round entirely.
Otherwise, flip it to the front only if it is not already there, then flip the whole region to send it to the end.

items: When only prefix reversal is allowed, two flips (to the front, then to a target boundary) can move any element to any position within the unsorted region.
This mirrors selection sort's "find the extreme value, place it at the boundary, shrink the region" structure, adapted to a prefix-flip-only toolkit.
Skipping a flip that would be a no-op (the target already being in the required position) is a simple, safe optimization for constrained-operation problems like this.

blocks.text: Pancake Sorting is solved with a selection-sort-style approach adapted to prefix flips: each round finds the largest unsorted element, flips it to the front if needed, then flips the whole unsorted region to send it to its final position, shrinking the unsorted region by one each round, using at most 2n flips total.
